studies.headline: Change the wallpaper, wake up your regulars: why small, unexplained store tweaks make loyal shoppers notice prices again
studies.the_study: Across two online shopping simulations and a field experiment in a local restaurant, researchers tested what happens when a familiar retail environment changes in a way customers cannot easily explain. Repeat customers normally stop paying attention to promotions as visits accumulate, but a random change in the background screen color of an online store made them more likely to notice and act on a price change, and a laser light added to a display case made loyalty customers more likely to spot a menu change and order the daily special. The key is ambiguity: the changes carried no information about which option was better, yet they reset attention.
studies.why_it_matters: Promotional messages lose power on exactly the customers retailers most want to move, and this suggests a cheap lever — periodic, meaningless-looking environmental change — to restore attention without discounting more deeply.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test whether rotating ambiguous store or site elements (background colors, lighting, fixture placement) before a price or assortment change lifts response among your most frequent shoppers — and conversely, whether holding the environment stable protects margins by keeping habitual buyers on autopilot. Two of the three studies were online simulations, so treat this as a hypothesis for an A/B test rather than a settled tactic.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your brain stops reading price tags in stores you visit often. The flip side: when something looks subtly off — new lighting, a rearranged shelf — you start looking again, which is precisely when retailers may be hoping to catch your eye.
studies.caveats: Two of three studies were online shopping simulations rather than real purchases; the field experiment was at a single local restaurant; effects on actual revenue over time were not established.
studies.paper_title: Managing the responsiveness of repeat customers to retail promotions: effects of ambiguous changes to the store environment

studies.headline: Donors are impatient too: charities promising help "soon" beat charities promising more help later
studies.the_study: Seven pre-registered experiments (N=2,462) plus an analysis of GoFundMe data tested whether people discount charitable impact the way they discount their own rewards. Participants consistently preferred donating to programs whose benefits would reach beneficiaries sooner — across causes, donation sizes, timeframes and charity sizes — and the preference held even when earlier impact meant trading off impact magnitude, charity quality rating, overhead or how close a campaign was to its goal. Beyond simple time discounting, earlier impact made donors infer the organization was more competent and trustworthy.
studies.why_it_matters: Nonprofits and cause-marketing partners routinely pitch long-horizon programs; this evidence suggests the timing of visible impact is itself a persuasion variable, and one that can override objective measures of effectiveness.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit how your fundraising or cause campaign communicates when money turns into results — making the first impact milestone sooner and more concrete may outperform messaging about larger eventual outcomes. The flip side is a credibility risk: a timing-first pitch can steer money away from higher-impact but slower programs, so watch for backlash if promised speed does not materialize.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When you give, you may be rewarding speed rather than effectiveness. The study found donors treated a faster payoff as a signal that the charity is trustworthy — a shortcut worth noticing next time a slower, larger-impact program fails to move you.
studies.caveats: Mostly online experiments with hypothetical donation choices rather than observed giving; the GoFundMe analysis is correlational secondary data.
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: Impatient for Impact: Intertemporal Preferences for Earlier Donation Impact Timing

studies.headline: Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do
studies.the_study: A controlled behavioral experiment with 360 participants generating 1,800 observations measured "green price tolerance" — the price premium at which people abandon a sustainable product for a conventional one — across five product categories and four conditions: no signal, a peer signal, an influencer/KOL signal, and an aggregate rating signal. All three social signals raised the switching threshold, with rating signals the strongest, then influencers, then peers. Tolerance also varied substantially by product category.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes the sustainability premium question from "will people pay more?" to "how much more before they defect?" — and suggests aggregate user ratings may be a cheaper lever on that threshold than influencer partnerships.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you carry a green price premium, test whether surfacing aggregate ratings at the point of choice extends the premium you can hold, and measure the threshold by category rather than assuming one sustainability premium across the portfolio. This was a single-market lab-style experiment, so treat the ranking of signal types as a hypothesis for live price testing.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers like to think their green purchases reflect values, but the experiment suggests a visible crowd verdict — a rating score — is what keeps them paying extra when the gap widens.
studies.caveats: Controlled experiment with choice tasks rather than real purchases; single emerging market; modest sample (360 participants across conditions); categories limited to five.
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.paper_title: Social signals and green price tolerance: experimental evidence across product categories

studies.headline: What 6,602 auctioned paintings reveal about who really sets the price in a chaotic market
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed transaction-level records for 6,602 paintings sold through a major European auction house between 2016 and 2024, comparing pricing dynamics before, during and after the pandemic. Intermediary pre-sale estimates — especially the lower estimate — tracked realized prices closely, and three of the models supported a pandemic-era price premium, while a persistent post-pandemic premium was not consistently supported.
studies.why_it_matters: In markets where goods are one-of-a-kind and buyers have no reference price, the intermediary's published estimate functions as the anchor that holds valuations together — a role that becomes more visible, not less, when markets are disrupted.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone selling unique or hard-to-compare items — art, collectibles, bespoke services, resale — the lesson is that your published estimate or guide price is doing most of the valuation work; consider how deliberately that anchor is set and whether crisis conditions warrant adjusting it. Findings come from one auction house, so generalization to other intermediaries is untested.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The pandemic did not permanently inflate art prices the way headlines suggested; the premium showed up during the disruption but did not clearly persist afterward.
studies.caveats: Single auction house in one region; observational data, so the intermediary-estimate link is associational rather than causal; pandemic premium supported in only some model specifications.
studies.paper_title: The Anchoring Role of Service Intermediaries During Crises

studies.headline: Stocking the shelves is not enough: a six-district study finds healthy food on sale but out of reach
studies.the_study: A convergent mixed-methods study across six districts of Paraguay combined retail audits of 26 establishments, surveys of 432 consumers, price analysis of 338 products, and field observations to test the assumption that making nutritious food physically available improves diets. Researchers found that broad availability coexisted with affordability constraints, highly variable pricing across retailers, uneven store organization, and household food routines that crowded out fruit and vegetables.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the "food desert" logic behind much food policy and retail siting: availability, affordability, store usability and cultural fit are four separate hurdles, and clearing only the first changes little.
studies.story_angle_primary: For grocery and CPG leaders working on health-oriented assortments in lower-income markets, the implication is that distribution metrics overstate reach — price dispersion across stores, shelf navigability and whether a product fits existing cooking routines all need separate measurement. Treat this as a framework drawn from one country rather than a quantified effect.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If fresh produce is in your local store and you still don't buy it, the research suggests that is less a personal failing than a stack of structural frictions — price variation between shops, how the store is laid out, and whether the food fits how your household actually cooks.
studies.caveats: Single country (Paraguay), small retail-audit sample (26 establishments), cross-sectional and largely descriptive/interpretive — no causal test of interventions.
studies.paper_title: Beyond Availability: Effective Access, Provisioning Systems, and Dietary Inequality

studies.headline: The Groupon customers everyone warned you about? They paid off within a year
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed purchase-history data from a company that ran a Groupon acquisition campaign restricted to prospective customers, tracking the long-run value of deal-acquired buyers against customers acquired through other channels. Despite losing money during the redemption window, the campaign delivered a substantial long-term return on investment. Groupon-acquired customers had lower lifetime value overall, but their spending was front-loaded, making them roughly as valuable as organically acquired customers in year one — and more valuable than organics the more heavily a firm discounts future income. Crucially, existing customers' lifetime value did not drop, because the firm honored redemption requests from current customers rather than policing eligibility.
studies.why_it_matters: Daily-deal and steep-discount acquisition has a reputation for buying worthless bargain hunters and insulting loyal customers; this transaction-level evidence suggests both fears can be managed, and that payback timing matters as much as total lifetime value.
studies.story_angle_primary: Re-examine how you judge discount acquisition campaigns: if your firm has a high cost of capital, front-loaded deal customers may beat slower-burning organic ones on a discounted-cash-flow basis. Also test the fairness lever — honoring deals for existing customers appears to be what prevented backlash here, though this is one company's campaign and worth replicating before scaling.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, it's a reminder that deal sites are an audition: companies are betting you'll spend heavily in the first year. And if you're already a customer, it can be worth asking whether a "new customers only" offer will be honored anyway — refusing is what generates resentment, and some firms know it.
studies.caveats: Single company and a single Groupon campaign, so generalization across categories is uncertain; observational purchase data rather than a randomized experiment, and the no-backlash result depends on this firm's specific redemption policy.
studies.paper_title: Effectiveness of daily deal acquisition campaigns and reactions by existing customers

studies.headline: Half of German consumers say they'd buy biodiversity-friendly food — and pay more for it
studies.the_study: Using a representative German survey sample (N=1,093) and latent profile analysis, researchers sorted consumers into five groups based on their acceptance of biodiversity-friendly food and the barriers holding them back. Three receptive segments — Biodiversity Enthusiasts (8%), the Environmentally Concerned (40%) and Low-Efficacy Supporters (6%) — together make up over half the population. The remaining consumers were Disinterested (36%) or Price Conscious (11%). Biodiversity attributes raised stated willingness to pay across all segments, including the less receptive ones.
studies.why_it_matters: Biodiversity is emerging as a sustainability claim distinct from carbon or organic, and this suggests a large addressable segment exists in a major European market — if labeling and wording are credible enough to be believed.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're building a sustainability claim beyond carbon, test biodiversity framing against your current labels — but note the big receptive group is "Environmentally Concerned," not activists, meaning the claim has to work for mainstream shoppers who need simple, credible proof. The "Low-Efficacy Supporters" segment is a specific communications problem: they care but doubt their purchase changes anything.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A new eco-label is coming to supermarket shelves, and it is not about carbon. Worth knowing what biodiversity claims actually certify before paying a premium for them.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey in a single country with stated willingness to pay rather than observed purchases; stated environmental intentions routinely overstate actual buying.
studies.paper_title: Who is buying biodiversity? Consumer target groups for biodiversity-friendly food

studies.headline: When AI agents do the shopping, prices fall — and platforms lose their grip on the shelf
studies.the_study: This is an analytical model, not a data study: the authors build a two-seller platform game in which a platform decides whether to grant AI shopping agents access and how to bias its rankings, while sellers choose prices, platform-facing visibility spending and agent-facing adaptation. Key results include that AI-mediated shopping pushes prices down when comparison pressure outweighs verified differentiation, that platforms may open information access while blocking transaction execution, and that the two kinds of visibility investment can flip from complements to rivals when agent and platform rankings disagree. The model also finds that the degree of openness a platform privately prefers can be worse for overall welfare than the socially optimal level.
studies.why_it_matters: Agentic commerce is arriving before anyone has evidence about how it reallocates traffic and margin, and this maps out the strategic logic a brand will face: optimizing for a human browsing a marketplace and optimizing for an AI buyer may soon be competing budget lines.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat agent-facing optimization as a separate investment with its own threshold, not an extension of SEO or retail media — and watch for platforms that let agents read listings but not complete purchases. Because this is a theoretical framework, use it to structure experiments on how your products surface to agents, not as a forecast.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If shopping bots become mainstream, the main consumer benefit may be lower prices from relentless comparison — but only for products whose differences can't be verified, which is exactly where brands will push back by making quality claims that only a human can judge.
studies.caveats: Purely analytical game-theoretic model with numerical extensions; no empirical data, no real consumers or transactions, and the pricing results depend entirely on modeling assumptions about comparison pressure and verifiable differentiation.
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.paper_title: AI shopping agents and the reallocation of consumer attention: seller visibility and platform access in agentic commerce

studies.headline: When cigarettes get pricier, smokers switch — but only if they haven't already vaped
studies.the_study: Researchers ran an experimental marketplace in the US in which adults completed simulated purchasing trials while cigarette prices rose step by step and alternative nicotine products were offered at half, one and two times market price. Participants were 25 people who smoke cigarettes only and 28 who both smoke and vape. Exclusive smokers substituted vaping products and heated tobacco for cigarettes as cigarette prices climbed, and treated nicotine pouches as a complement — buying more of both — when pouches were cheap. For dual users, cigarette purchases barely budged regardless of price or what else was on the shelf.
studies.why_it_matters: Cross-price effects decide whether a tax or price increase moves people to lower-risk products or simply costs them more, and this shows the answer depends entirely on which consumer segment you are looking at.
studies.story_angle_primary: A reminder for anyone pricing across a product portfolio: the same price increase can trigger substitution in one segment and nothing at all in another, and a cheap adjacent product can behave as a complement rather than a rival. Worth testing cross-price elasticity by user type, not just in aggregate, before assuming a price move will steer demand where you want it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It shows how habits harden around price: people who had already added vaping to their routine kept buying cigarettes no matter what they cost, while single-product users were much more price-sensitive and easily nudged toward alternatives.
studies.caveats: Small sample (25 and 28 participants) in a within-subject design; purchases were made in a simulated experimental marketplace rather than with real money in real stores; single country (USA); registered trial NCT05177848.
studies.paper_title: Substitution and complementarity among tobacco products: an experimental marketplace study in the USA

studies.headline: Nearly 730,000 days of Airbnb data show deep learning can forecast demand — and explain itself
studies.the_study: Researchers assembled 729,888 daily observations from 1,852 Airbnb listings in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and pitted traditional forecasting methods (regression, SARIMAX) against neural network architectures including LSTM, Transformer and a hybrid. The deep learning models clearly outperformed the traditional baselines, and the team layered on SHAP attribution to show which features drove each prediction, then simulated three-by-three pricing games between competing hosts across four submarkets.
studies.why_it_matters: Revenue managers often reject machine-learning pricing tools because they cannot explain the output; pairing accurate forecasts with feature-level attribution and competitor-response simulation makes the black box auditable.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are evaluating algorithmic pricing or demand forecasting vendors, ask not just for accuracy benchmarks but for feature attribution and competitive-response modeling — knowing a rival's likely counter-move matters as much as the forecast itself.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The nightly price on a short-term rental is increasingly the output of a model playing a strategic game against the model next door, rather than a host's judgment about a quiet Tuesday.
studies.caveats: Single city (Ann Arbor, Michigan) and a single platform; the pricing game is a simulation, not observed host behavior; largely a modeling and methods contribution rather than a substantive finding about consumers.
studies.journal: Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management
studies.paper_title: A 2-layered game-theoretic deep learning model for predicting lodging demand: SHAP and nash equilibrium

studies.headline: When explaining your algorithm backfires: short beats thorough on AI disclosure
studies.the_study: Two between-subjects online scenario experiments with adult consumers from a South Korean research panel (Study 1 N=392, crossing disclosure level with explanation type and product context; Study 2 N=220, a 2x2 design) tested how much platforms should say about why an AI recommended a product. Trust was highest when a single-sentence explanation accompanied the recommendation — higher than no explanation at all, and higher than when technical and procedural detail was piled on. In Study 2, identical detailed disclosure content lowered perceived authenticity and trust, via heightened skepticism, when it was framed as image-oriented ("we're an AI-first company") rather than as serving the shopper.
studies.why_it_matters: Platforms and retailers are racing to bolt "explainable AI" language onto recommendation widgets and product pages, on the assumption that more transparency equals more trust; this evidence suggests elaborate disclosure can read as marketing spin and erode the very trust it was meant to build.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat AI disclosure as copy, not compliance: A/B test a one-line "because you viewed X" explainer against your fuller technical disclosure and watch click-through and conversion, not just trust surveys. Also audit the framing — language that positions AI as a brand credential rather than a shopper service may trigger skepticism. These are scenario experiments on a panel, so they show what can happen, not what will happen on a live storefront.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful consumer heuristic: when a site goes out of its way to tell you how clever its algorithm is, that's often promotion rather than disclosure. The study found shoppers instinctively discount heavy AI talk as "AI-washing" — doubt about whether the AI claims are real at all.
studies.caveats: Online panel; hypothetical scenarios rather than real purchases; stated trust and purchase intention rather than observed behavior; single country (South Korea); Study 2's cells are small (N=220 across four conditions); the role of skepticism in the elaborated-disclosure effect was not clearly supported in Study 1.
studies.paper_title: When Is AI Recommendation Transparency Read as Promotion? Disclosure Elaboration, Motive Attribution, and Consumer Trust

studies.headline: Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy: confrontational apps cut what farmers demand to change practice
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a discrete choice experiment with irrigated fruit farmers in the Region of Murcia, Spain, asking them to choose among packages combining three climate adaptation practices (subsurface irrigation, regulated deficit irrigation, cover crops) with a monetary incentive — framed either as a subsidy or a discount — and one of four nudge types delivered via app or certification: facilitators (advisory apps), confrontational (apps showing the consequences of not adopting), social norms (peer benchmarking), and reinforcement (public recognition and certification). Both money and nudges raised willingness to adopt, and the nudges reduced the compensation farmers required. Confrontational nudges were the most effective; facilitation nudges produced heterogeneous responses, and social-norm and signaling nudges gave no clear effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a price on behavioral design: a well-chosen information intervention substitutes for part of a cash incentive, which matters to anyone — policymaker, agricultural input supplier, or B2B marketer — trying to shift professional buyers' behavior without raising the discount.
studies.story_angle_primary: The transferable idea for pricing teams is substitution between incentive and information: if a message can lower the discount needed to trigger adoption, the message has a measurable monetary value you can quantify. Worth testing whether loss-framed, consequence-showing content outperforms peer-comparison content in your category — the social-proof nudge, a marketing default, underperformed here. Note this is a stated-choice study, so the price reductions are modeled, not booked.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Peer pressure is the nudge everyone reaches for, but in this sample of farmers it did essentially nothing, while being shown the concrete downside of inaction moved people most. It is a reminder that what persuades experts making costly professional decisions differs from what persuades shoppers.
studies.caveats: Stated preferences in a hypothetical choice experiment, not observed adoption; a single region (Murcia, Spain) and a single sector (irrigated fruit farming); sample size not reported in the abstract; findings may not generalize to consumer markets.
studies.paper_title: Climate change adaptation practices in fruit-irrigated agriculture: the role of nudging in farmers’ adoption decisions

studies.headline: Feeling powerful makes people pay less when they get to name their own price
studies.the_study: Researchers tested how a consumer's momentary sense of power shapes what they voluntarily hand over under pay-what-you-want pricing, drawing on the agentic-communal model of power. Across their studies, people primed into a high-power state paid less than those in a low-power state, and the effect ran through orientation: power pushed people toward agentic, self-focused thinking rather than communal, other-focused thinking. Crucially, the gap closed when social motivation was made salient — under those conditions high-power consumers actually paid more. The published abstract does not report sample sizes, nationality or whether participants paid real money.
studies.why_it_matters: Pay-what-you-want and "name your price" models live or die on voluntary generosity, and this suggests the framing around the payment moment — not just the customer's wallet — determines the number they type in.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you run a tip-prompt, donation add-on or name-your-price checkout, this is a cue to A/B test social framing ("your payment supports the people who made this," visible community averages) against neutral framing — especially in contexts that make customers feel in control, such as premium tiers, VIP status or heavy-customization flows, which may be quietly suppressing what people pay. Treat it as a hypothesis to validate on your own traffic, not a settled result.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The next time a checkout screen asks you to choose your own price or tip, notice what happened just before: being made to feel like the one in charge tends to shrink what people give, while a reminder that a real person is on the other end tends to expand it. Your "fair price" is more situational than it feels.
studies.caveats: Abstract reports no sample size, participant pool, country or study design details, and gives no indication whether payments were real or hypothetical; mechanism is established via mediation analysis, which is correlational even within experiments; findings are framed around priming power states, a literature with known replication debates.
studies.journal: Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management
studies.paper_title: The effect of consumers’ power states on pay-what-you-want pricing

fact_check.headline: Change the wallpaper, wake up your regulars: why small, unexplained store tweaks make loyal shoppers notice prices again
fact_check.notes: Design (two online simulations plus one restaurant field experiment), mechanism (ambiguity) and both manipulations match the abstract; caveats correctly note the simulation-heavy evidence base.

fact_check.headline: Donors are impatient too: charities promising help "soon" beat charities promising more help later
fact_check.notes: Seven pre-registered experiments (N=2,462) plus GoFundMe secondary data, the tradeoff list and the efficacy-based trust mechanism all match; the digest's abbreviation of the tradeoff list (it omits "number of prior donors") is signalled by "or" and does not mislead.

fact_check.headline: Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do
fact_check.notes: Sample (360 participants, 1,800 observations), five categories, four signal conditions, the ranking of signal effects and the category variation all match the abstract; caveats correctly note the single emerging market and choice-task design.

fact_check.headline: What 6,602 auctioned paintings reveal about who really sets the price in a chaotic market
fact_check.notes: Data, period and model results reported accurately; one consumer-facing line converts "not consistently supported" into a positive claim that no lasting premium exists.

issues.label: Absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence
issues.as_written: The pandemic did not permanently inflate art prices the way headlines suggested; the premium showed up during the disruption but did not clearly persist afterward.
issues.abstract_says: Pandemic premiums are supported in three models, whereas a persistent post-pandemic premium is not consistently supported.
issues.problem: "Did not permanently inflate" asserts a null result, whereas the abstract reports only that a persistent premium was not consistently supported across model specifications. The second half of the sentence hedges correctly, but the opening clause overstates.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "The evidence for a lasting post-pandemic price premium was inconsistent across models; the premium showed up clearly only during the disruption."

fact_check.headline: Stocking the shelves is not enough: a six-district study finds healthy food on sale but out of reach
fact_check.notes: All component figures (26 establishments, 432 consumers, 338 products, six districts of Paraguay) match, the four dimensions are correctly reproduced, and the digest flags the descriptive/interpretive nature of the work.

fact_check.headline: The Groupon customers everyone warned you about? They paid off within a year
fact_check.notes: Design, ROI finding, front-loading and the fairness/redemption-policy explanation all match; one clause upgrades "relative value increased" into an outright reversal of ranking.

issues.label: Relative value overstated as outperformance
issues.as_written: and more valuable than organics the more heavily a firm discounts future income
issues.abstract_says: their relative value increased with a firm's discount rate of future incomes
issues.problem: The abstract says only that the relative value of Groupon customers rises as the discount rate rises; it does not state that they overtake organically acquired customers at any point. The digest asserts a crossover the abstract does not report.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to "and their value relative to organics rose the more heavily a firm discounts future income."

fact_check.headline: Half of German consumers say they'd buy biodiversity-friendly food — and pay more for it
fact_check.notes: Sample, method and all five segment percentages match exactly; small causal-sounding verb on a survey association, plus a speculative claim about labels reaching shelves.

issues.label: Causal verb for a survey association
issues.as_written: Biodiversity attributes raised stated willingness to pay across all segments, including the less receptive ones.
issues.abstract_says: Across all target groups biodiversity-friendly product attributes are associated with higher stated willingness to pay
issues.problem: This is a cross-sectional survey with latent profile analysis; "raised" implies an experimentally demonstrated effect rather than the association the abstract reports.
issues.suggested_fix: Change "raised" to "were associated with higher" stated willingness to pay.

issues.label: Speculation beyond the abstract
issues.as_written: A new eco-label is coming to supermarket shelves, and it is not about carbon.
issues.abstract_says: the market potential for these products and the characteristics of relevant consumer target groups remain unclear ... making communication, wording, and credible labelling decisive for market success
issues.problem: The abstract studies consumer acceptance and segment potential; it makes no claim that a biodiversity label is arriving in stores. The forecast is the digest's own.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe as "Biodiversity could become the next sustainability claim on supermarket shelves — this study suggests the audience for it exists."

fact_check.headline: When AI agents do the shopping, prices fall — and platforms lose their grip on the shelf
fact_check.notes: Correctly identified as an analytical two-seller platform model with numerical extensions; the four headline results (price effects, layered access, complements-to-rivals flip, private vs social openness) all track the abstract, and caveats state clearly that there are no data.

fact_check.headline: When cigarettes get pricier, smokers switch — but only if they haven't already vaped
fact_check.notes: Sample sizes, design, price manipulations and the exclusive-smoker substitution/complementarity pattern match; the dual-user result is stated more absolutely than the abstract supports and one abstract finding is dropped.

issues.label: Dual-user null stated too absolutely
issues.as_written: people who had already added vaping to their routine kept buying cigarettes no matter what they cost
issues.abstract_says: Individuals who smoke cigarettes and use NVP purchased more NVP and less HTP with no significant effects of cigarette price ... for individuals who smoke cigarettes and use NVP, cigarette purchasing was not affected by the availability of other products
issues.problem: The abstract's conclusion about dual users concerns cigarette purchasing being unaffected by the availability of other products; "no matter what they cost" turns a non-significant result in a 28-person sample into a definitive statement about price insensitivity.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to "cigarette purchasing among dual users showed no significant response to the other products on offer, and price effects were not detected in this small sample."

issues.label: Dropped dual-user finding
issues.as_written: For dual users, cigarette purchases barely budged regardless of price or what else was on the shelf.
issues.abstract_says: Individuals who smoke cigarettes and use NVP purchased more NVP and less HTP with no significant effects of cigarette price.
issues.problem: The abstract reports that dual users did shift between alternatives (more vaping products, less heated tobacco); the digest presents them as entirely unresponsive, omitting that within-alternative movement.
issues.suggested_fix: Add that dual users still shifted between alternatives — buying more vaping products and less heated tobacco — even though cigarette purchases did not move.

fact_check.headline: Nearly 730,000 days of Airbnb data show deep learning can forecast demand — and explain itself
fact_check.notes: Observation count, listing count, city, model comparison and the SHAP/Nash two-layer structure all match; the digest omits that the simple FCNN, not the LSTM/Transformer architectures it names, was the best performer and the basis for the pricing game.

issues.label: Best-performing model omitted
issues.as_written: pitted traditional forecasting methods (regression, SARIMAX) against neural network architectures including LSTM, Transformer and a hybrid
issues.abstract_says: we compare traditional models (regression, SARIMAX) with advanced architectures (FCNN, LSTM, Transformer, and a Transformer–LSTM hybrid) ... The best-performing model (FCNN) was further used to simulate a 3x3 pricing game
issues.problem: By naming only LSTM, Transformer and the hybrid, the digest implies these were the winning models, when the abstract identifies the simpler FCNN as best-performing and as the model used for the pricing game — a relevant detail for anyone drawing a vendor-evaluation lesson.
issues.suggested_fix: Name FCNN in the model list and note that it was the best performer and the model used for the 3x3 pricing simulation.

fact_check.headline: When explaining your algorithm backfires: short beats thorough on AI disclosure
fact_check.notes: Design, Ns and both studies' core results match the abstract closely; the consumer angle overstates the AI-washing skepticism result, and an illustrative quote is not in the abstract.

issues.label: AI-washing skepticism overstated in consumer angle
issues.as_written: The study found shoppers instinctively discount heavy AI talk as "AI-washing" — doubt about whether the AI claims are real at all.
issues.abstract_says: The trust advantage of a brief explanation over no explanation was accompanied by lower AI-washing skepticism, reflecting doubts about AI claims, whereas Study 1 provided no clear evidence that skepticism accounted for the lower trust under elaborated disclosure. In Study 2 (N = 220; 2 × 2 design), identical high-disclosure content lowered perceived authenticity and trust, through heightened skepticism, when framed as image-oriented rather than consumer-serving.
issues.problem: Skepticism explained the trust drop only for image-oriented framing in Study 2; Study 1 found no clear evidence it drove the elaborated-disclosure effect. Presenting it as a general, instinctive consumer reaction goes beyond the abstract and sits awkwardly against the digest's own caveat.
issues.suggested_fix: Rewrite as: "In one study, when detailed AI talk was framed as a brand credential rather than a service to the shopper, it raised 'AI-washing' skepticism and lowered trust — though the evidence for that mechanism was not consistent across both studies."

issues.label: Illustrative quote not in abstract
issues.as_written: when it was framed as image-oriented ("we're an AI-first company") rather than as serving the shopper
issues.abstract_says: identical high-disclosure content lowered perceived authenticity and trust, through heightened skepticism, when framed as image-oriented rather than consumer-serving
issues.problem: The quoted wording is an invented example presented as if it were stimulus material; it cannot be verified from the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop the quotation marks or mark it as the digest's own paraphrase, e.g. "framed as image-oriented (brand-credential language) rather than as serving the shopper".

fact_check.headline: Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy: confrontational apps cut what farmers demand to change practice
fact_check.notes: Design, nudge categories and the ranking of effects match the abstract; the characterization of social-norm nudges as doing "essentially nothing" firms up an "undefined" result.

issues.label: "Undefined" results described as a null effect
issues.as_written: Peer pressure is the nudge everyone reaches for, but in this sample of farmers it did essentially nothing
issues.abstract_says: Confrontational nudges are most effective; facilitation nudges show heterogeneous response and social influence and signalling nudges generate undefined responses.
issues.problem: "Undefined responses" means the direction/effect was not clearly identified, which is not the same as a demonstrated null. The body text ("gave no clear effect") is accurate, but the consumer angle hardens it into "did essentially nothing" and "underperformed".
issues.suggested_fix: Change to "produced no clearly identifiable effect in this sample" in both the consumer angle and the marketer angle.

fact_check.headline: Feeling powerful makes people pay less when they get to name their own price
fact_check.notes: Direction of the main effect, mediator and social-motivation moderation match the abstract, but the digest asserts priming and multiple studies that the abstract does not state, and describes the gap as closing rather than narrowing.

issues.label: Design details (priming, multiple studies) not in abstract
issues.as_written: Across their studies, people primed into a high-power state paid less than those in a low-power state
issues.abstract_says: The results show that individuals with a high sense of power pay less than individuals with a low sense of power in pay-what-you-want contexts and that the agentic–communal orientation mediates the effect of power states on the payment.
issues.problem: The abstract never says power was manipulated by priming or that there were multiple studies; the digest elsewhere concedes that no design details are reported, so the body contradicts its own caveat.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "people with a high sense of power paid less than those with a low sense of power" and note that the abstract does not specify how power states were induced or how many studies were run; drop "primed" and "Across their studies" or mark them as unverifiable.

issues.label: "Gap closed" overstates a narrowing
issues.as_written: Crucially, the gap closed when social motivation was made salient — under those conditions high-power consumers actually paid more.
issues.abstract_says: when social motivation is salient, individuals with a high sense of power pay more and the payment difference between low-power and high-power individuals decreases
issues.problem: The abstract reports the difference decreasing, not disappearing; "the gap closed" implies elimination.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to "the gap narrowed when social motivation was made salient — high-power consumers paid more under those conditions".

sections.trends:
**Convergent findings**
- **Transparency is not linearly good — the mediator is perceived deception or skepticism.** "When explaining your algorithm backfires: short beats thorough on AI disclosure" (W7225591358) lands directly against last run's "When hidden fees sting" (W7214557291). One shows that withholding information until checkout produces betrayal; the other shows that piling on technical detail — especially when framed as a brand credential — produces "AI-washing" skepticism and lowers trust below the one-line explanation. Together they define a narrow optimum: early, brief, shopper-serving disclosure.
- **Price formation where there is no list price now has quantitative backing.** "What 6,602 auctioned paintings reveal about who really sets the price in a chaotic market" (W7224345056) picks up the thread opened last run by "What actually sets the price of a used record" (W7212042826) and "When a price is called a donation" (W7207733471), but with transaction-level data: the intermediary's published estimate is the anchor doing the work a price tag normally does, and it holds through disruption.
- **Price sensitivity is segmented by disposition, not just budget.** "When cigarettes get pricier, smokers switch — but only if they haven't already vaped" (W7225156193) converges with "Shy shoppers are more price-conscious" (W7223569994): in both, the same price environment produces opposite responses from subgroups, and the aggregate elasticity hides the story.
- **Environmental and interface design keeps moving demand with no price change.** "Change the wallpaper, wake up your regulars" (W7225627982) is the physical-store counterpart to last run's "Take away the filters and shoppers buy pricier, more varied products" (W7223129134) — ambiguous, non-informative design changes reset attention to price exactly as filter removal reset breadth of search.

**Advances**
- The platform-as-price-setter model line advances from creators to machines. "When AI agents do the shopping, prices fall — and platforms lose their grip on the shelf" (W7224901915) is the successor to "Why a platform might hand its influencer rivals better tools" (W7220981580): both are game-theoretic models in which a platform's decision about how much capability to grant an intermediary is really a decision about who pays. The new model adds the possibility that platforms open information access while blocking transaction execution.
- Acquisition-economics evidence deepens. "The Groupon customers everyone warned you about? They paid off within a year" (W7225402212) extends "Delivery subscriptions nearly double spending" (W7222938569) from membership to deep-discount acquisition, and sharpens it: the useful metric is the *timing* of cash, not total lifetime value.
- Algorithmic pricing moves from "is it accurate" to "can it be audited." "Nearly 730,000 days of Airbnb data show deep learning can forecast demand — and explain itself" (W7167636549) advances last run's methodological warning in "Your conjoint study's willingness-to-pay number may be an artifact of how you coded price" (W7221780439): both say the invisible modeling layer is where pricing decisions are actually made, and the new study offers feature attribution plus competitor-response simulation as the governance fix.
- Stated willingness to pay stays fragile. "Half of German consumers say they'd buy biodiversity-friendly food — and pay more for it" (W7225468467), "Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do" (W7221815863) and "Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy" (W7225388749) all rest on stated or simulated choice, reinforcing the caution established by W7221780439.

**Counterpoints**
- **Social proof, marketing's default lever, underperformed twice this run.** In "Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do" (W7221815863), peer signals were the weakest of three social cues and aggregate ratings the strongest; in "Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy" (W7225388749), social-norm and public-recognition nudges produced no clear effect while confrontational, consequence-showing content worked best. That sits awkwardly with the influencer-centric logic of W7220981580, where influencer effectiveness is the asset platforms are deciding whether to unlock.
- Deal-driven acquisition is partly rehabilitated. The previous run's framing of discounting as a trust and margin liability (W7221330457, W7214557291) gets a counterweight in W7225402212, where a heavily discounted Groupon cohort delivered substantial long-run ROI and no erosion of existing customers' value — conditional on the firm honoring deals for current customers rather than policing eligibility.

**New themes**
- **Temporal discounting in giving:** "Donors are impatient too" (W7224975922) introduces time-to-impact as a persuasion variable that overrides charity quality ratings — no precedent in the previous digest.
- **Pay-what-you-want and the psychology of the payment moment:** "Feeling powerful makes people pay less when they get to name their own price" (W7213671471) opens voluntary pricing as a topic; its closest prior relative is the donation vocabulary of W7207733471, but the mechanism is new.
- **Availability versus affordability in access markets:** "Stocking the shelves is not enough" (W7225110412) brings macromarketing and food-policy pricing into the topic for the first time.
- **Agentic commerce as a pricing regime:** W7224901915 is the first study here to treat AI buying agents as a channel with its own visibility budget.
sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** Three studies in this batch find that the classic peer-and-influencer persuasion toolkit is the weakest lever on what people will pay, while aggregate, institutional, or consequence-based signals do the heavy lifting. Aggregate star ratings extended the sustainable-product price premium further than influencer endorsements, with peer signals weakest of all ("Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do," W7221815863); peer-benchmarking and public-recognition nudges had no clear effect on farmers while apps showing the consequences of inaction cut the cash incentive needed most ("Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy," W7225388749); and in a one-of-a-kind market with no reference price, the intermediary's published estimate — not crowd sentiment — tracked what buyers actually paid ("What 6,602 auctioned paintings reveal about who really sets the price in a chaotic market," W7224345056). "When explaining your algorithm backfires" (W7225591358) adds the flip side: when a brand speaks loudly about its own credibility, shoppers discount the claim.

**Why pitch this now:** Creator and influencer budgets are still climbing as a share of marketing spend just as AI shopping agents and tightened fake-review enforcement make machine-readable aggregate ratings the dominant input into what a shopper or a bot sees first.

**Angle:** A reported feature on where price-justifying credibility now comes from — testing the industry's assumption that a human voice persuades better than a number, and asking what happens to influencer budgets when the signal that actually holds a premium is an aggregate score a brand cannot script. Aimed at brand and media-buying decision-makers, with a consumer-facing version on the mental shortcuts people use to decide a higher price is fair.

**Potential headlines:**
- A star rating held a green price premium longer than an influencer did
- Marketing's favorite persuasion lever, peer pressure, keeps losing to a number
- What you actually trust when you decide a higher price is worth it

**Potential outlets:**
- **Marketing Week** — has an audience of brand-side marketers actively defending or cutting creator budgets, and this is an evidence-based challenge to where that money goes.
- **Digiday** — covers the creator-economy spend debate closely and would take the reallocation question from influencer fees toward ratings and review infrastructure.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — the broader governance argument, that credibility signals a firm does not control outperform ones it buys, suits its management-research register.
- **Fast Company** — runs consumer-behavior and business-culture pieces, and the "the influencer loses to the star rating" turn works for a general business readership.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **Change the wallpaper, wake up your regulars (Work ID W7225627982):** A cheap alternative to deeper discounting — rotating meaningless store or site details before a price change wakes habitual shoppers out of promotional blindness, for a retail trade explainer, with a consumer-psychology sidebar on why you stop reading price tags where you shop most.
- **Donors are impatient too (Work ID W7224975922):** Donors rewarded speed of impact over size of impact and read fast payoff as proof of competence, overriding charity ratings — for a nonprofit/cause-marketing trade piece and a general-interest personal-giving column timed to year-end fundraising.
- **Star ratings buy more green premium than influencers do (Work ID W7221815863):** Reframes the sustainability premium as a defection threshold and ranks the cheapest way to raise it, for a CMO-audience column on sustainability pricing or a retail media trade piece.
- **What 6,602 auctioned paintings reveal about who really sets the price (Work ID W7224345056):** The published pre-sale estimate is doing the valuation work in markets with no reference price — plus the debunk that the pandemic art-price boom did not clearly persist, for a business/arts-market news piece or a resale-commerce explainer.
- **Stocking the shelves is not enough (Work ID W7225110412):** Distribution metrics overstate reach when price dispersion, store layout, and household cooking routines each block purchase independently, for a grocery/CPG trade feature on emerging-market health assortments or a food-policy explainer challenging food-desert logic.
- **The Groupon customers everyone warned you about? They paid off within a year (Work ID W7225402212):** Deal-acquired customers were front-loaded spenders who beat organics once you discount future cash — and honoring "new customers only" deals for existing customers is what prevented backlash, for a marketing-trade news brief or a CFO/CMO column on acquisition payback.
- **Half of German consumers say they'd buy biodiversity-friendly food (Work ID W7225468467):** Biodiversity is emerging as a sustainability claim separate from carbon, with a mainstream rather than activist receptive segment, for a food and grocery trade piece or a consumer explainer on what a new eco-label actually certifies.
- **When AI agents do the shopping, prices fall (Work ID W7224901915):** Agent-facing optimization is a separate budget line from retail media and SEO, and platforms may let agents read listings while blocking them from buying — for an e-commerce or ad-tech trade analysis, clearly flagged as a theoretical model.
- **When cigarettes get pricier, smokers switch — but only if they haven't already vaped (Work ID W7225156193):** Cross-price elasticity split sharply by user type, with cheap nicotine pouches acting as a complement rather than a substitute, for a tobacco/health-policy news piece and a portfolio-pricing column on why aggregate elasticity misleads.
- **Nearly 730,000 days of Airbnb data show deep learning can forecast demand — and explain itself (Work ID W7167636549):** A buyer's checklist for algorithmic pricing vendors — demand feature attribution and competitor-response simulation, not just accuracy benchmarks, for a revenue-management or hospitality trade piece, with a consumer angle on nightly rates set by models playing against each other.
- **When explaining your algorithm backfires (Work ID W7225591358):** Treat AI disclosure as copy, not compliance — one line beat both silence and a full technical explanation, and "AI-first company" framing triggered skepticism, for a marketing-trade news brief or a product/UX column aimed at teams bolting explainability onto recommendation widgets.
- **Nudges can buy down the price of a subsidy (Work ID W7225388749):** Information has a measurable monetary value because the right message lowers the incentive needed to trigger adoption — and the social-proof nudge, marketing's default, did nothing, for a B2B marketing column or an agricultural/policy trade explainer.
- **Feeling powerful makes people pay less when they get to name their own price (Work ID W7213671471):** VIP tiers, customization flows, and other control-conferring experiences may be quietly suppressing what customers volunteer at tip prompts and name-your-price checkouts, unless social framing is added, for a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet or a pricing-practitioner column, with the abstract's missing method details flagged.
